"Every Old Car Has Rust": Owner Sells 1958 Chevrolet Impala Parked for Too Many Years
9 photos
Photo: Facebook Marketplace
Every old car has rust. This is how the owner begins the description of this Impala, trying to justify the obvious corrosion you’ll find on the car.
This 1958 Impala has been sitting for God knows how long, so it’s now a project that needs complete restoration. That’s why it’s here in the first place. It needs to convince someone online to take it home, begin a complete restoration, and bring it back to the road.
The owner doesn’t share many specifics, so my recommendation from the get-go is to call them and ask all your questions. A walkaround video is a good place to start, but if you’re interested in an Impala that can be parked in your collection, an in-person inspection is necessary.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace The 1958 model year is without a doubt the most collectible Impala ever released. It was the first Impala, with Chevrolet needing just two years to bring this nameplate from the drawing board to the production channel.
Presented in 1956 as a concept at GM’s motor show, the Impala graduated to a production model in 1958. It was part of the Bel Air lineup and could be had as a convertible or as a hardtop.
The Impala was a successful release from the very first days on the market. It immediately generated impressive excitement, eventually propelling Chevrolet to the leading spot in the American car space. The GM brand ended the year with over 1.25 million cars sold to local buyers, whereas Ford , the company which until that point dominated the domestic automotive industry, fell to second place with 1.03 million cars.
The Impala was not an affordable car. The hardtop started at $2,586, while the base convertible carried a price tag of $2,724.
The Impala was offered with a wide range of engines, as Chevrolet wanted the new car to appeal to as many buyers as possible. The base choice was a 235 six rated at 145 horsepower, while the 283, which debuted only a year earlier, represented the entry in the V8 series. The 283 was offered in multiple more powerful choices, including with 270 horsepower if buyers were willing to pay $183 more.
The 348 was the big news of the year, as it represented the big-block option full-size Chevy buyers were waiting for. The 348 also joined the lineup with several configurations, including the highly-desirable Special Turbo-Thrust Tr-Power with 315 horsepower.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace This Impala landed on Facebook Marketplace without much information. Unfortunately, reading the door plate is quite difficult, considering its current condition, so it’s impossible to tell what engine is hiding under the hood - if an engine is still there, in the first place.
The seller claims that most of the parts are still there, so it’s probably safe to assume that an engine is also available. I wouldn’t expect this Impala to be fitted with a 348, as this would have been a major selling point, and not mentioning it in the listing would be quite a mistake.
Otherwise, this Impala is by all means a restoration project. It suffers from obvious rust damage, and the seller says this is no different from other old cars. I don’t think this is true, as many old cars that have been babied and stored inside are now spotless, even without a previous restoration.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace This Impala has been parked for many years, and this explains its current condition. That’s why I recommended that you request a walkaround video or go there in person, as assuming that this Impala can be restored to day-one specifications is impossible without additional details.
I can’t help but insist on the obvious part: this is a 1958 Impala, and these cars are becoming rarer. Keeping them original should be a priority, especially if the right engine is under the hood. Not everybody likes a six, but a 1958 Impala that still has the factory-installed 235 is a fantastic car, even if it’s not worth as much as a 348-powered sibling.
The six was a good choice for someone who wanted to drive the Impala daily, and I would always choose a 235 over a non-original engine.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace As for the price of this Impala, I can’t say I’m surprised, but I think the owner should have offered more information about the car and what you can find under the hood. They want $13,500 for this Impala, so give them a call and see what this mysterious hardtop is all about.
If you don’t live very far from Jurupa Valley, California, paying the owner a visit is probably the right thing to do if you’re committed to a purchase. It’s unclear if the Impala can move on its own, so for the time being, you should also consider shipping costs, especially if the vehicle must go on a long trip to reach your garage.
